Senses.Explanation: Chan records deploy Layman Fu through a small set of repeated cases, verses, and writings. Their own identification says he lived at Yunhuang Mountain, planted two trees called the Twin Grove, and called himself the Future Layman Shanhui. His central public case has Liang Emperor Wu invite him to lecture on the Diamond Scripture: Fu strikes the desk once and leaves the seat; when the emperor says he does not understand, Zhigong says, 'the layman has finished lecturing.' Masters repeatedly quote and criticize his sayings. One address cites 'if you wish to know where buddha goes, it is only this voice,' then says Fu did not distinguish good from bad. Another says Fu only knew how to wash while clinging to a bridge pillar and release a boat, adding that this was stamped from a printing block and released from a mold. A biography records a monk awakening at words from Fu's Heart-King Inscription: 'the taste of salt in water, blue pigment in color—decidedly present, its form unseen.' A portrait inscription calls him neither Confucian, Daoist, nor Chan and criticizes his made-up conduct. His verse 'empty-handed I hold a hoe; walking, I ride an ox; a person crosses over the bridge; the bridge flows, the water does not' also circulates widely. The Zen deviation is this figure's life in the record as lecturer who strikes and leaves, quoted author, verse speaker, portrait subject, and target of masters' criticism—not a general biography of Fu.
Senses.Note: Exact count: 551 hits in 173 allowlisted texts. Layman-Fu-lectures (傅大士講) has 34 hits in 29 texts; Heart-King Inscription by Layman Fu (傅大士心王銘) 27 in 17; empty-handed holding a hoe (空手把鉏頭) 35 in 22; striking the desk once (揮案一下) 32 in 25. One person sense. Layman Fu is an invoked pre-lineage figure, not a Chan lineage master roster entry.

Occurrences.Kwic: 梁武帝請傅大士講金剛經大士便於座上。揮案一下。便下座武帝愕然誌公問。陛下還會麼帝云。不會誌公云。大士講經竟。
Occurrences.AttributionNote: Central public case: invited lecture, one desk strike, departure from the seat, and Zhigong's verdict.

Occurrences.Kwic: 大士者。居雲黃山。手栽二樹。謂之雙林。自稱當來善慧大士。
Occurrences.AttributionNote: In-corpus identification: Yunhuang Mountain, Twin Grove, and his self-applied title.

Occurrences.Kwic: 諸禪德，大小傅大士祇會抱橋柱澡洗，把󳮪放船，印板上打將來，模子裏脫將去。

AlternateTargets: a bronze head and iron brow
Senses.Explanation: Literally, “bronze-headed and iron-browed.” Chan texts use the compact bodily description as an epithet for unusually formidable people, especially monks imagined as able to withstand severe encounter. One hall address places “bronze-headed and iron-browed” directly under “the patch-robed monk's gate.” Verses nevertheless say that even such a fellow receives a welt from one staff-blow, or stands bloodied under the staff's command. Elsewhere the phrase itself answers “What is buddha?”, followed by the equally concrete “bird's beak and fish's gills.” These occurrences establish the epithet and its Chan setting; they do not establish literal metal anatomy or an occult quality. The headword occurs 208 times across 114 allowlisted texts.
Senses.Note: Adjectival and substantivized uses refer to the same kind of formidable person and do not require separate senses.

Occurrences.Kwic: 十地心驚，二乘罔測，衲僧門下，銅頭鐵額
Occurrences.AttributionNote: A hall address places the bronze-headed and iron-browed under the patch-robed monk's gate.

Occurrences.Kwic: 問：如何是佛？師云：銅頭鐵額。僧曰：意旨如何？師云：鳥觜魚腮
Occurrences.AttributionNote: In public interview the phrase answers “What is buddha?”, followed by “bird's beak and fish's gills.”

Occurrences.Kwic: 縱使銅頭鐵額漢，也須一棒一條痕
Occurrences.AttributionNote: A verse on Deshan says even a bronze-headed, iron-browed fellow must bear one welt from one blow.

Occurrences.Kwic: 銅頭鐵額漢，盡在此山中
Occurrences.AttributionNote: A verse says the bronze-headed, iron-browed fellows are all within this mountain.

Occurrences.Kwic: 一棒施行該百令，銅頭鐵額血淋身
Occurrences.AttributionNote: An entering-room verse puts the epithet under one staff-blow and describes the body as bloodied.
